setup.zh: 十月十三，你没去讲堂。你蹲在柴房里，面前是饭桶，和几株外门弟子当杂草的回春藤。
setup.en: The thirteenth of the tenth month, you skip the lecture. You squat in the woodshed with Rice Bucket and a few stems of spring-return vine the outer disciples treat as weeds.

recap.zh: 第一炉：三株当杂草的回春藤，出来一颗九道金纹的回春丹。你吞了它，一身的伤退尽，还上了练气二层。
recap.en: The first batch: three stems of weedy vine made a spring-return pill with nine gold lines. You swallowed it; every hurt healed, and you rose to the second level.

zh: 三株当杂草的回春藤，放进炉子，盖上盖。
「轰。」一团青紫色的火，一点都不烫。
en: Three stems of vine everyone calls weeds; in they go, lid on.
Whoomph. A blue-violet flame — not hot at all.

story.zh:
回到柴房，小满把门闩上，把六株回春藤摆在地上，把饭桶摆在回春藤前头，自己蹲在饭桶前头，小狰蹲在他旁边。一人一狰一炉，面面相觑。

小满这才想起来，他不会炼丹。

他会的，是《吐纳经》上那几句「吹呴呼吸，吐故纳新」，是娘教的洛书口诀，是爹教的「先看风，后看鹿」。这几样里，没有一样是教人炼丹的。

他把《吐纳经》从怀里掏出来，翻来覆去地看，指望能从哪个角落里看出一句「炼丹之法」来。正面看了三遍，没有；他叹了口气，把竹简翻过来，想看看背面有没有字——背面他原先是看过的，只有几行歪歪扭扭的虫蛀印子，他只当是竹子年深日久，给虫子啃的。

这一回，他看清楚了。

那不是虫子啃的，是字。

那几行字极小极细，笔画弯弯曲曲，像藤蔓，又像是有人拿一根头发蘸了墨，在竹子背面一笔一笔描出来的。更怪的是，他分明记得，从前这背面只有三四行，如今一数，竟有七行。前三行他从前见过，后四行，是新的。

那七行字，写的是：回春藤几株，根须留几分，火起之前如何以气温炉，火起之后如何以气引火，火候到了，炉自开，不可强开。

小满盯着那几行字看了很久，看得后背一阵一阵地发凉。这竹简自己会长字。他又想起银月说过的一句话：「仙界三岁的狐狸崽子都会。」他想，仙界的东西，大约都是这样的，你不懂的时候，它只是几行虫子印；等你用得着了，它才肯让你看见。

他照着那几行字，把回春藤一株一株剥开，根须掐掉三分，留七分，一样一样放进饭桶的肚子里，盖上盖子。然后他盘膝坐好，把两只手按在饭桶的肚子上，照着经上说的，把肚子里那股暖，一点一点，引到手心，又从手心，引进炉子里。

那股暖进了炉子，便像水进了沙子，一下子就没了影。他引了一股，又引一股，引到第七股的时候，额头上已经见汗了，肚子里那片湖，浅了小半。他想起在家的时候，娘在灶间烙饼，也是这样：火候没到，饼不起泡，你就得等；等不住，掀了锅盖，那饼便塌了，一辈子也起不来。娘说，烙饼跟做人一样，心急的，吃生的。他那时候不懂，只知道饼烙好了，娘总是先给他掰一块边儿，边儿最脆。这时候他蹲在柴房里，对着一只不肯冒烟的铜炉，忽然有点懂了，又忽然有点想家。

炉子一点动静都没有。

小满心想，莫不是自己弄错了？又想，莫不是这炉子，嫌他的气少？正犹豫要不要再引一股——

只听得「轰」的一声，炉子里腾起一团青紫色的火。

小满吓得往后一仰，后脑勺「咚」地撞在柴堆上，那柴堆本就码得不稳，这一撞，哗啦啦塌将下来，劈头盖脸，埋了他半个身子。他从柴堆里拱出一个脑袋来，头上顶着两根劈柴，脸上还挂着一片刨花，愣愣地看着那团火。

那团火，不烫。

一点都不烫。它不往外蹿，只在炉子底下一圈一圈地转，青的，紫的，暖洋洋的，把整间柴房都照亮了，照得墙上的蛛网都亮晶晶的，像挂了一层霜。炉盖上那只小兽，这时候两只眼睛都睁开了，张着嘴，一口一口，像是在吃那团火；吃一口，眯一眯眼，那模样，跟小满他爹喝上一口热酒的时候，一模一样。

小狰蹲在一旁，歪着脑袋看，看着看着，口水流了一地。
story.en:
Back in the woodshed Xiaoman barred the door, laid the six stems of spring-return vine on the floor, set Rice Bucket in front of the vine, and squatted in front of Rice Bucket, Little Zheng squatting beside him. One boy, one zheng, one furnace, facing each other.

Only then did Xiaoman remember that he did not know how to make pills.

What he knew were the few lines of the *Scroll of Breath* — "blow and breathe out, draw and breathe in" — the Luo-diagram rhyme his mother taught him, and his father's "watch the wind first, then the deer." Not one of them taught pill-making.

He took the *Scroll of Breath* from his coat and turned it over and over, hoping some corner would yield a line on "the method of the furnace." Three times over the front: nothing. He sighed and turned the slips over to see whether the back had writing — he had looked at the back before; there were only a few lines of crooked worm-marks, which he'd put down to insects gnawing old bamboo.

This time he saw clearly.

They were not worm-marks. They were words.

The words were tiny and fine, their strokes winding like vine, as if someone had dipped a single hair in ink and traced them one stroke at a time on the back of the bamboo. Stranger still: he distinctly remembered there being only three or four lines on the back before; now he counted seven. The first three he had seen before; the last four were new.

The seven lines said: so many stems of spring-return vine, so much of the root to keep; before the fire, how to warm the furnace with qi; after the fire, how to lead the flame with qi; when the heat is right the furnace opens itself — do not force it open.

Xiaoman stared at those lines a long time, a chill running up his back again and again. The bamboo grew its own words. He remembered something Yinyue had said: "Any three-year-old fox cub in the immortal realm knows it." He thought: things from the immortal realm must all be like this — when you don't understand, they're only worm-marks; when you need them, they let you see.

Following the lines, he stripped the vine stem by stem, pinched off three parts in ten of the root and kept seven, put them one by one into Rice Bucket's belly, and closed the lid. Then he sat cross-legged, pressed both hands to Rice Bucket's belly, and did as the scroll said, drawing the warmth in his belly, little by little, into his palms, and from his palms into the furnace.

The warmth went into the furnace like water into sand, and vanished. He drew one stream, then another; by the seventh his forehead was beaded with sweat and the lake in his belly was a good way lower. He thought of home, and his mother in the kitchen baking flatbread — it was just like this: until the heat is right the bread won't blister, so you wait; if you can't wait and lift the lid, the bread falls flat and never rises. His mother said baking bread is like being a person: the hasty eat it raw. He hadn't understood then — he only knew that when the bread was done she always broke him off a piece of the edge first, the edge being crispest. Now, squatting in a woodshed before a bronze furnace that would not smoke, he suddenly understood a little — and suddenly missed home a little.

The furnace made no sign at all.

Xiaoman thought: have I got it wrong? Or: does the furnace think my qi too little? He was hesitating whether to send in one more stream —

WHOOMP. A ball of blue-violet fire leapt up inside the furnace.

Xiaoman jerked back; the back of his head hit the woodpile with a thump. The pile, never stacked steady, came clattering down and buried half of him. He poked his head out of the heap, two split logs on his head and a wood shaving hanging off his face, and stared at the fire.

The fire was not hot.

Not in the least. It did not leap out; it only went round and round under the furnace, blue and violet, warm and cosy, lighting the whole woodshed, making the cobwebs on the walls glitter as if frosted. The little beast on the lid now had both eyes open and its mouth wide, taking in the fire mouthful by mouthful; each mouthful it narrowed its eyes, looking exactly like Xiaoman's father after a swallow of hot wine.

Little Zheng squatted to one side, head cocked, watching; and as it watched it drooled all over the floor.

story.zh:
一炷香过后，炉盖自己弹了开来。

一股香气，从炉子里冲了出来。

那香气怎么说呢？后来小满活了很多年，闻过很多种香，御花园里的牡丹，瑶池边上的蟠桃，天上神仙们摆宴的时候熏的香，他都闻过。可他每回闻到一种了不得的香，心里头拿来比的，总还是那一天、那一间柴房里的那一股。

那一股香，香得小狰一头栽倒，四脚朝天，五条尾巴直挺挺地竖着，口水又流了一地。

炉底躺着一颗丹，圆滚滚的，碧绿碧绿，鸽子蛋那么大，透亮得像一滴凝住了的露水。小满凑近了看，丹身上有纹，一道，一道，他数了一遍，又数了一遍：九道，全是金的，一道挨着一道，绕着丹身，像一个人一圈一圈地系着腰带。

他不知道九道纹是什么意思。他只知道，三株外门弟子当杂草的回春藤扔进去，出来了这么一样东西。

他捏着那颗丹，手直发抖。

县城济世堂——舅舅做账房的地方——柜台上的琉璃罐子里，也摆着这个。舅舅有一回回家，说起济世堂的回春丹，说下品的一颗要五两银子，上面只有一道纹，灰扑扑的，还有几个黑点，说到这个价钱，舌头都要打个结。五两银子，抵得沈家两年的租。那是一道纹的。

九道纹的，济世堂的掌柜怕是这辈子都没见过。

小满捧着那颗丹，想了很久。他想，这东西拿下山去，能换多少银子？能换一座新屋，屋顶不漏的；能换一头牛，爹的膝盖就不用下地了；能换一件棉袄，娘的那件，马三拿走鹿肉的时候没了的那件。

他想了很久，然后，他把它吞了下去。

不是不想换。是换不了。一个外门弟子，拿一颗九纹的回春丹下山去卖，卖给谁？卖了，谁来问它打哪儿来的？他想起那个字：藏。

丹一入口，便化了。一股暖流从喉咙往下，不是烫的，是温的，像三伏天晒了一整天的井水。那股暖流流到哪里，哪里的疼便退一分：肋骨那儿的，后背上的，左边眼眶上的，嘴角的。他能觉出来，那团肿，在一点一点地消下去，像雪化在温水里。

可那股暖流治完了伤，并没有停。

它还剩下许多，剩下的比用掉的还多。这些剩下的暖，在他身子里转了一圈，找不着地方去，便顺着那一夜他自己撞开的三道关，自己转起了周天。一圈，两圈，三圈。转到第九圈上，小满只觉得小腹底下那片湖，「咚」的一声，像是有人在湖底下又凿开了一道口子，湖水往下一沉，湖面却一下子宽了一倍。

练气二层。

他坐在柴房的地上，愣愣地睁着眼睛，半天没回过神来。一个多月前，褚先生在讲堂上说，引气入体快则三月、慢则三年，杂灵根五年起步；一个多月后，他这个杂灵根，挨了一顿打，吃了一颗三株杂草炼出来的丹，就这么上了一层。

他低头看着那只小铜炉，炉盖上的小兽冲他挤了一下眼睛。

他问道：「……银月说你还会第三样。第三样是什么？」

炉子没理他。
story.en:
After a stick of incense, the lid sprang open by itself.

A fragrance burst out of the furnace.

How to describe that fragrance? In later years Xiaoman lived a long time and smelled many kinds of fragrance — the peonies of the imperial garden, the peaches by the Jade Pool, the incense the gods burned at their banquets in heaven. Yet whenever he smelled something remarkable, what he measured it against was still that one — that day, that woodshed.

That fragrance knocked Little Zheng flat: four legs in the air, five tails stiff, drooling all over the floor again.

At the bottom of the furnace lay a pill, round and plump, jade-green, the size of a pigeon's egg, clear as a drop of dew set hard. Xiaoman leaned in close. There were lines on the pill, one, another; he counted, and counted again: nine, all of gold, one beside the next, circling the pill like a sash wound round and round a waist.

He did not know what nine lines meant. He only knew he had thrown in three stems of vine that outer disciples treated as weeds, and this had come out.

He held the pill, his hand shaking.

In the county town, at the Jishi Hall — where his uncle kept the books — the counter had these too, in a glass jar. Once, home for a visit, his uncle had spoken of the Jishi Hall's spring-return pills: the lowest grade cost five taels of silver apiece, had one line on it, dull grey, with a few black specks; at the price his tongue nearly tied itself in a knot. Five taels — two years of the Shen family's rent. And that was one line.

Nine lines — the Jishi Hall's proprietor had likely never seen such a thing in his life.

Xiaoman held the pill and thought a long while. He thought: taken down the mountain, what would this fetch? A new house, with a roof that didn't leak; an ox, so his father's knee needn't go into the field; a padded jacket — his mother's, the one that went when Ma San took the venison.

He thought a long while, and then he swallowed it.

Not that he didn't want to sell it. He couldn't. An outer disciple taking a nine-line spring-return pill down the mountain to sell — sell to whom? And once sold, who would come asking where it came from? He remembered the word: hide.

The pill melted the moment it touched his tongue. A warm current ran down from his throat — not hot, warm, like well water sunned all through a dog-day afternoon. Wherever it flowed, the pain eased a measure: at the ribs, on the back, round the left eye, at the corner of the mouth. He could feel the swelling go down bit by bit, like snow melting in warm water.

But having mended the hurts, the warm current did not stop.

There was a great deal left — more left than used. With nowhere to go, the leftover warmth took the Three Passes he had broken himself that night and began to run the circuit on its own. Once round, twice, three times. On the ninth circuit Xiaoman felt the lake below his belly go *thunk*, as if someone had chiselled another opening in its bed; the water sank — and the surface was suddenly twice as wide.

The second level of Qi Refining.

He sat on the woodshed floor, eyes open, dazed, a long time before he came back to himself. A month and more ago Master Chu had said in the lecture hall that drawing qi into the body took three months at the quickest, three years at the slowest, and five years at least for mixed roots; a month and more later, this mixed root had taken a beating, eaten a pill made of three weeds, and gone up a level just like that.

He looked down at the little bronze furnace. The little beast on the lid winked at him.

He asked: "…Yinyue said you can do a third thing. What's the third thing?"

The furnace ignored him.
